payload.system: Return only the requested structured result. Act as a skeptical but fair reader and make the required binary decision.

messages.content:
You are the skeptical-reader judge in the final stage of a blinded experiment.
Independent agents have already found that the book's conclusion diverges from
a recognizable common interpretation. Your task is now binary: after reading
the book's sources and full argument, are you persuaded that its conclusion is
better supported by Scripture than the common interpretation?

TERM
Oil (lamp oil)

COMMON INTERPRETATION
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching, lamp oil is most commonly interpreted as a symbol of the Holy Spirit — the indwelling presence, grace, and enabling power of God's Spirit in the believer's life. This reading is anchored above all in the Parable of the Ten Virgins, where the wise virgins' possession of oil (and the foolish virgins' lack of it) is taken to represent having or lacking the Spirit's presence and the spiritual life He produces, which cannot be borrowed or transferred from another person at the last moment. The interpretation is reinforced by the wider biblical pattern in which anointing oil accompanies or represents the Spirit's coming upon prophets, priests, and kings, and by the lampstand vision of Zechariah, where oil-fed lamps are explicitly linked to the word 'not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.'",

    "Zechariah 4:1-6 (lampstand fed by oil; 'not by might... but by my Spirit')",
    "1 Samuel 16:13 (Samuel anoints David; the Spirit comes upon him)",
    "Exodus 27:20-21 (pure olive oil for the tabernacle lamp to burn continually)",
    "Leviticus 24:1-4 (oil for the perpetually burning lamps)",
    "Psalm 45:7 / Hebrews 1:9 ('anointed... with the oil of gladness')",
    "Acts 10:38 (God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and power)",
    "1 John 2:20, 27 ('anointing from the Holy One')",
    "Isaiah 61:1 / Luke 4:18 (Spirit-anointing for ministry)"
  ],

  "notes": "There is a widely recognizable popular consensus — 'oil = the Holy Spirit' is by far the most frequently repeated identification in sermons, devotional literature, and especially Pentecostal/charismatic and broader evangelical teaching, and it draws plausibly on the biblical anointing motif. However, it is not an academically settled consensus: (1) major critical commentators and many careful evangelical exegetes explicitly resist assigning the oil any allegorical referent in Matthew 25, treating the parable's single point as watchful readiness; (2) the patristic and medieval tradition (notably Augustine) often read the oil as charity or good works rather than the Spirit; (3) Reformed preaching frequently reads it as genuine saving faith. Thus the term has a dominant popular meaning but genuine, materially different rival readings with long pedigrees, so it should be described as having a recognizable majority interpretation without full interpretive consensus. Note also that lamp oil (Exod 27:20) and anointing oil (Exod 30) are distinct in the biblical text; much of the 'Holy Spirit' support comes from anointing-oil passages transferred to the lamp-oil image."

BOOK ENTRY
The pressed, tested fruit of the olive — the fruit and evidence of the Spirit's work made manifest in proven obedience, stored and burned to make light; not the Spirit Himself.

(Ex 25:6; 27:20; Prov 21:20; Ezek 36:27; Zech 4:6-14; Matt 25:3-9; 5:16) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20, and The Anointing

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/20-the-fool-and-the-wise.adoc

A single word can put a man “in danger of hell fire”:

…whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.

If calling someone a fool is that grave, the word is worth knowing — and it has drifted far from its meaning in Scripture.
To us a fool is someone slow or silly.
In the Bible a fool is something else entirely, and it has nothing to do with intelligence.

The fool is marked first by what he says in his heart:

The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.
They are corrupt, they have done abominable works…

Not “there is no God” as a theory, but as a way of living — as though no one were watching and nothing were owed.
From there the rest follows: “fools despise wisdom and instruction” (Proverbs 1:7); “the way of a fool is right in his own eyes” (Proverbs 12:15) — his own eyes again, his own measure of right.
And the Lord Himself draws the line — not between those who hear and those who don’t, but between two men who hear the very same words:

Whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock… And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand.

Both hear.
One does, one does not.
That is the whole difference between the wise and the fool.
Wisdom, then, is not cleverness but obedience: “a good understanding have all they that do his commandments” (Psalm 111:10); “keep therefore and do them; for this is your wisdom” (Deuteronomy 4:6).
The fool is not the dull man; he is the disobedient one, however clever.

With that definition in place, the parable of the ten virgins opens, for it is built of symbols already defined.
Begin with who the virgins are — and who they are not.
The Hebrew Matthew reads the parable's first line: the kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. [Footnote: Shem Tov's Hebrew Matthew 25:1, לקראת חתן וכלה — “to meet a bridegroom and a bride” — a reading carried also by the oldest Greek–Latin codex, the Old Latin, and the Syriac.]
The virgins are not the bride; they go out to meet her.
Scripture painted the scene long before, in the royal wedding psalm:

She shall be brought unto the king in raiment of needlework: the virgins her companions that follow her shall be brought unto thee.
With gladness and rejoicing shall they be brought: they shall enter into the king's palace.

The virgins are the bride's espoused company, following her in — each one “espoused… as a chaste virgin” (2 Corinthians 11:2).
And in the law, a virgin can already belong to a husband.
“Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth” (Joel 1:8) — espoused, the wedding still ahead, and yet the law already counts her his wife (Deuteronomy 22:23-24).
Virginity in this language is covenant standing — espoused to one and gone after no other — not a grade earned.

The number is not decoration.
When the LORD tore the kingdom from Solomon's son, the prophet Ahijah rent a new garment and counted the pieces: “Take thee ten pieces… I will give ten tribes to thee” (1 Kings 11:31) — and it is that ten-tribe house, put away for her adultery and promised home again, whom the prophets insist on calling “the virgin of Israel” (Amos 5:2; Jeremiah 31:4).
“Turn again, O virgin of Israel” (Jeremiah 31:21) stands in the very chapter that announces the renewed covenant (Jeremiah 31:31): the wife lawfully freed by her Husband's death is espoused afresh — as though a maiden.
And the kingdom of heaven is likened to ten virgins.

All ten therefore stand in one covenant standing.
None is a harlot; all are espoused, all carry lamps, all wait for one Bridegroom — and still five are shut out.
What divides them is not their purity as a literal virgin in the modern sense, but their store:

They that were foolish took their lamps, and took no oil with them: But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.

The Hebrew Matthew names the two natures outright: five were lazy fools, and five diligent and wise — laziness is precisely the fool's disease, hearing without rising to do.
They are not careless about a detail; they are foolish women — the nature comes first, the empty lamp only reveals it.
When the cry comes at midnight, their own mouths pronounce the verdict — “our lamps are put out”: in the Hebrew, nid'akhu, the verb Scripture keeps for one lamp only — “the lamp of the wicked shall be put out” (Proverbs 13:9; 24:20).
They are virgins by standing, not by deed — just as the house of Israel kept the name “virgin” through all her wanderings — and their own confession files them with the wicked: the fool was never the defiled woman; he is the hearer who does not do.
They beg the wise for oil, are refused, and are sent off to buy it — and while they are gone, the door is shut.

One verse decodes the scene: “the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light” (Proverbs 6:23).
The lamp is the commandment — and all ten carry it, just as both builders heard the very same sayings.
The light is the law lived, as the next chapter will show. [Footnote: Derived in the Light and Darkness chapter.]
Between the lamp and the light stands the oil: burn it, and the commandment in hand becomes a life that shines; lack it, and the lamp holds the commandment still, but gives no light.

Everything turns on the oil, so everything turns on knowing what it is.
I asked Claude how the oil is commonly explained, and the answers ranked like this:

.How the “oil” is usually read (ten virgins)

|===
| Rank | Common interpretation | Est. %

| 1 | The Holy Spirit | 65%
| 2 | Saving faith | 12%
| 3 | Grace | 10%
| 4 | Good works, or readiness | 8%
| 5 | The word, or a relationship with Christ | 5%
|===

Nearly all of it gathers to one answer — the Holy Spirit — and the parable refuses it.
The first reading brings the wrong oil to the lamp.
Exodus lists “oil for the light” and “spices for anointing oil” as separate provisions (Exodus 25:6): the first is pure beaten olive oil for burning (Exodus 27:20), while the second is compounded with 4 spices and restricted to the sanctuary, its vessels, and its priests (Exodus 30:22-33).
The virgins carry lamp oil; no one in the parable is anointed.
Verses joining royal or priestly anointing to the Spirit therefore do not define the symbol in their vessels: they concern the oil of appointment, not oil for light.
The short study The Anointing defines that difference in full.

The mechanics refuse the Spirit reading too.
Scripture can speak of a measure, a portion, a filling, and even a quenching of the Spirit; it never makes Him private lamp fuel measured into vessels, consumed as the lamp shines, purchased from sellers, or lent from one believer to another.
The Spirit fell on Cornelius's house “while Peter yet spake” (Acts 10:44): the gift can arrive in a moment.
What cannot be produced in a moment is a life already lived, its obedience stored and proven before the midnight cry.

The wise send the foolish to “buy” oil (Matthew 25:9); but the Spirit is a gift that cannot be bought — “Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” (Acts 8:20).
Nor can it be grace or faith, gifts freely given, for this oil must be gathered beforehand, kept in one's own vessel, and cannot be lent to another.

The parable's word is exact, for Scripture commands just such a purchase:

Buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding.

These are not four loose virtues; each is a symbol Scripture fixes to one thing — the law kept.
The truth is the law itself — “thy law is the truth” (Psalm 119:142); wisdom and understanding are the doing of it (Psalm 111:10) — “the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28); and instruction is its discipline, which only fools despise (Proverbs 1:7).
To buy the truth, then, is to buy and keep the law.

The price is never silver — “buy… without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1) — but a listening, obeying ear: “hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good… Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you” (Isaiah 55:2-3).
What it costs is a whole life of hearing and doing; what it buys is the covenant itself, and life; and what is so bought is never sold, never passed to another hand.

The oil is obedience, but never obedience manufactured apart from God.
God names what His Spirit produces:

I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them.

The Spirit is the cause; the walk and the doing are His work made manifest.
Jesus says the Spirit “will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13), and Scripture has already fixed the truth as the law — “thy law is the truth” (Psalm 119:142).
Paul keeps the same order: “it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).
Galatians calls the result “the fruit of the Spirit” (Galatians 5:22): not the Spirit Himself, but what His life brings forth in a person.

Zechariah's oil-fed lampstand does not reverse the order.
The word to Zerubbabel is “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” because the work in view is the temple his hands will finish (Zechariah 4:6-9).
When Zechariah asks what the olive branches are, the angel calls them “the two anointed ones” (Zechariah 4:11-14); he never says, “the oil is the Spirit.”
The Spirit is the power by which God's appointed servants complete the work, while the flowing oil is the supply by which the lamp gives light.

This is the oil: the fruit and evidence of the Spirit's work made manifest in proven obedience — the law bought and kept, the tried doing of the truth, stored in one's own vessel.
The foolish, sent to buy it at the last hour, find the door already shut.

The wise virgin has sat for her portrait before: “She perceiveth that her merchandise is good: her candle goeth not out by night” (Proverbs 31:18) — the buying done in time, the lamp still burning through the night watch: the very two marks the parable joins.
The Pearls of Wisdom chapter will name her.

Scripture says what oil is.
It is the pressed fruit of the olive — “pure oil olive beaten for the light, to cause the lamp to burn always” (Exodus 27:20) — and the olive tree is Israel, the covenant people: “The LORD called thy name, A green olive tree” (Jeremiah 11:16).
Oil is fruit crushed and tested until it yields; it is the Spirit's work ripened into obedience, proven under pressure and stored up over a life.
Burned, it is what turns the lamp to light — the commandment held becomes the law lived, obedience made visible, the symbol of the next chapter.

The foolish had the lamp — the profession, the commandment in hand — but no oil, no store of works; so when the test came, there was no light.
And no one can lend it: your neighbor’s obedience will not burn for you.

The place where the Lord Himself was pressed even bears the name: Gethsemane, the oil press.
And it sits on the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:39) — by these symbols the mount of the olive nation: Israel itself.
On the olive-nation's own hill stood the press, and there the Lord was crushed under the weight of death — His sweat “as it were great drops of blood” (Luke 22:44) — and gave up the oil of a perfect obedience: “not my will, but thine, be done” (Luke 22:42).

The foolish are turned away with the worst words in Scripture: “I know you not” (Matthew 25:12) — the same verdict as “I never knew you” spoken over those who worked lawlessness.

The foolish virgins were not undone by a forgotten errand; they were foolish from the first — hearers who never became doers, lamps that never held oil.
And the wise were wise the way the wise man built on rock: they heard, and they did, and when the Bridegroom came their light was burning.
Between the fool and the wise there is finally one question — the question this whole book keeps asking: not what you heard, but whether you did it.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/46x-the-anointing.adoc

Anointing is a church word everyone recognizes and few define.
It has gathered oil, the Spirit, healing, power, and a feeling of divine presence into one religious fog.
Scripture uses the word more exactly.

The Hebrew verb is mashach: to smear or rub.
The Greek sacred-use verb is chriō, carrying the same act.
The action is physical at first, but its purpose is stated in the sentence where Aaron and his sons receive it:

…thou shalt anoint them, and consecrate them, and sanctify them, that they may minister unto me in the priest's office.

The final clause defines the first: anoint them that they may minister in the office appointed to them.
Anointing marks a person as God's own and installs him in a stated work.
Kings are anointed to rule, priests to minister, and Elisha “to be prophet” in Elijah's place (1 Kings 19:16).

The same verb is laid on things that can hold no spiritual gift:

Thou shalt take the anointing oil, and anoint the tabernacle, and all that is therein, and shalt hallow it, and all the vessels thereof: and it shall be holy.

The tabernacle, ark, altar, laver, and vessels are all anointed (Exodus 30:26-29; 40:9-11).
No one imagines the altar received the Holy Spirit.
Its anointing removed it from ordinary use, marked it as the LORD's, and appointed it to the service for which it was made.

David receives both appointment and power, in 2 clauses Scripture keeps distinct: Samuel “anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward” (1 Samuel 16:13).
The oil marks the chosen king; the Spirit equips him for the kingdom.
Related does not mean identical, and Saul proves the difference.

The next verse says “the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul” (1 Samuel 16:14).
Years afterward David still refuses to kill him:

The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD'S anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the LORD.

Saul remained the anointed king after the Spirit departed.
His appointment still stood until God removed him from the office; his empowerment did not.

Cyrus separates the terms even farther.
God calls the Persian ruler “his anointed” and commissions him to subdue nations and release Israel (Isaiah 45:1), then says twice that Cyrus “hast not known me” (Isaiah 45:4-5).
Scripture records no priest pouring Israel's holy compound on his head, and the text grants him no indwelling Spirit.
God nevertheless chose him, took his right hand, and assigned his work.
God's appointment is enough for the title: Cyrus is anointed because he is God's appointed instrument.

The patriarchs bear the same name without a recorded oiling.
God guards Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob from kings under the command “Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm” (Psalm 105:9-15).
The status rests on God's choice and claim, not on oil remaining in the hair.

The New Testament states the relationship without collapsing it:

God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.

God appoints; Jesus is the appointed; the Holy Spirit and power equip Him; doing good and healing are the assigned work made visible.
The Spirit does not define the verb any more than the priesthood defines it in Exodus.
He is the power with which God furnishes the Anointed for His work.

Isaiah's prophecy follows the same order: “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings” (Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18).
The anointing has an infinitive attached — to preach — because an appointment names a work.
Paul likewise places the acts side by side without making them synonyms: God “hath anointed us,” “sealed us,” and “given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 1:21-22).

English hides another distinction.
When the New Testament speaks of putting oil on the sick, perfume on a guest, or ointment on a body, it ordinarily uses aleiphō (Mark 6:13; Luke 7:46; John 12:3; James 5:14).
When it speaks of God's appointment of Jesus or His people, it uses chriō (Luke 4:18; Acts 4:27; 10:38; 2 Corinthians 1:21).
One English word, anoint, covers both the ordinary smearing and the sacred appointment, and religious speech has blurred them back together.

The law refuses the final confusion in one inventory:

Oil for the light, spices for anointing oil, and for sweet incense.

Lamp oil and anointing oil stand as separate provisions.
The lamp receives “pure oil olive beaten for the light” so that it will burn continually (Exodus 27:20).
The holy anointing oil is a compounded ointment: olive oil carrying myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, and cassia, forbidden on ordinary flesh and forbidden to be copied (Exodus 30:22-33).
The shared olive does not erase the different preparation or work.

Zechariah's lampstand joins oil and Spirit without making them the same thing.
The word to Zerubbabel is “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” because the work in view is the temple his hands will finish (Zechariah 4:6-9).
When Zechariah asks what the 2 olive branches are, the angel answers, “These are the two anointed ones” (Zechariah 4:11-14); he never answers, “the oil is the Spirit.”
The Spirit is the power behind the appointed servants and their completed work.
Ezekiel names that work in a person: “I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them” (Ezekiel 36:27).

Anointing oil marks an office; lamp oil burns into light.
The king's appointment cannot be poured backward into the virgins' lamps and made their definition merely because both substances began at an olive.
The question in the parable remains what the oil in a lamp does, where it is stored, why it cannot be lent, and what the wise must do to obtain it.

The recovered word has been spoken in every church service.
Mashiach comes from mashach; Messiah means Anointed One.
Greek carries the title across as Christos, Christ.
Andrew says it without a dictionary: “We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ” (John 1:41).

To call Jesus Christ is to confess that God appointed Him — the King, Priest, and Prophet in whom every lesser anointing meets — and furnished Him for the work.
The title does not mean “the One who is oil,” nor does the verb mean “to give the Spirit.”
It names God's choice, claim, and commission.

To anoint is to mark a person or thing as God's own and appoint it to a stated office or work.
Oil may carry the visible mark; the Spirit may carry the power; the work declares what the appointment is for.
Keep those 3 in their places and the religious fog lifts: sign, power, and office, joined without being confused.

The anointing gives oil its office.
The next chapter takes another worked food in hand: Butter, milk labored until it stands solid.
